notes: Quick buttons on the planting form put a crop in half or a third of a bed without typing centimetres: top, middle or bottom down its length, or left, middle or right across its width (under “Side by side”).

Crops can now grow side by side in strips down a bed, such as peas along both edges with spinach down the middle. On the planting form, open “Side by side” and give each crop part of the width. Strips next to each other don’t count as sharing space.

Bed drawings now show the plants that are really there. Harvesting asks how many plants you pulled up (tap the ones that came out), and they leave the drawing. Delete the harvest and they come back. For crops you pick over a season, like peas, it starts at 0.
Ticking off thinning asks how many plants are left, or you can use the thinning distance as before. Tick “Always do it this way” to stop being asked; change it in Tools → Settings → Garden map.
If fewer seedlings went in than a plan had room for, the drawing shows only those. Where the drawing differs from the plan, a switch above it shows the plan instead.
Planting out can take seedlings from more than one batch of the same crop, such as 8 pots and 2 that were potted on later. Tap the other batch under “Seedlings going in”.
Dragging plants is easier on a phone. Touching near a plant is enough to pick it up, Zoom makes the drawing up to 3× bigger, and dragging a plant down no longer refreshes the page.

Planning or planting from your seedlings now asks how many go in. It starts with what the layout takes (a diamond takes 4, and peas go in pairs, so 8), shows them in the picture, and you can drag each one to where it will go.

Seedlings you don’t use stay in the tray, with their “Plant out” job, until you plant them somewhere else or discard them. A plan only sets aside the number it uses, so the rest can go into another plan.

Your seedlings are only suggested for a free space when they would be ready to plant out while it’s free and give a first picking at least two weeks before the next crop goes in. On the planting form the others are folded away with the reason.
The bottom bar now has the Season plan in place of the Log. The running log is on the Calendar page.

A bag’s potting mix no longer says it was filled on the day you added the bag to the app when a crop was already growing in it: the fill date moves back to that crop’s planting date. Bags you’ve already added are put right when you update.
Adding a pot or bag with its potting mix now asks when the mix went in.

No feeding in the run-up to harvest: the last feed is 4 weeks before for potatoes and other tubers, onions and garlic, 3 weeks for carrots, daikon and other roots, and 2 weeks for most other crops. Feeds planned later say “too close to harvest” with a Skip button. Crops picked over a long season, like tomatoes, keep being fed.

Potatoes and other tubers stop getting watering jobs 10 days before harvest so the skins firm up for storing; onions and garlic 2 weeks before so the necks dry. The crop page says so. Carrots and other roots keep steady watering, since a dry spell then a soaking splits them.

The garden map is gone: the Beds view does its job. Find a bed or crop by name, sort by name, what needs attention, driest, closest to harvest or newest sowing, and filter to what needs attention, is ready to pick, is dry or is empty.
Each card says what its coloured dot means (for example “Probably dry” or “Ready to harvest”), and a key above the cards explains the colours. Overdue jobs count as needing attention too.
“Sun & Moisture” on the Beds view shows each bed’s sun and how wet it probably is (or what the meter read today).
Areas such as Farm and Backyard: switch between them at the top of the Beds view, and add, rename or delete them from the Areas button.
Test site only: Tools → Fill with a made-up garden, for trying things out with beds, bags and seedlings at every stage.

The Garden tab has two views: Today (the forecast, crop alerts and today’s jobs) and Beds (a card for each bed and pot, with how far along each crop is and its next job). It remembers the one you used last.
Tap a day in the forecast to see that day’s crop risks and jobs; tap Today to see everything again.
Jobs the weather gets in the way of say so, for example “23mm rain tmrw” on watering, with a Skip button. Skipping a feed or spray moves it to the next dry day.
Beds and pots show a coloured dot for anything that needs you: amber for heat or dry soil, blue for rain, frost or wind, terracotta for ready to pick.
Bed and crop pages show the crop family, your latest pH reading and what you’ve dug in this year. Bed drawings start smaller, with a Bigger button.
The harvest window is a bar from sowing to past its best, with today marked. The “Pick by” job now keeps to its date as the forecast moves it, and says when it’s overdue.
Seedling checks show how many have come up against the 70% target, with a + to log a new count. The + button opens a quick log: harvest, emergence, feed or spray, and note or photo.
New line icons in place of the coloured emoji, and more even spacing in forms. The Garden map tile left Tools, since the map is on the Garden tab.
Dark theme: the rotation plan’s “not until” chips and its “anything can go here” line are readable, as are the “Striped” key on the season plan and the seedling details when planting.
Cream theme: hints, labels and small grey text are a little darker, so they’re easier to read.
Dark theme: the spray days list is readable again, as are search highlights, held crops on “OK to pick?”, and the plan, cover and warning chips.
Spray and pest tips no longer name a particular brand.

Your location’s usual weather (temperatures, rainfall and frost dates, which set the sowing months) now comes from the app’s own world climate map, made from the ERA5 records for 2016–2025: one small download for your area, once, with nothing asked of a weather service. It allows for your garden being higher or lower than the surrounding land, and frost dates were checked against weather-station records around the world.
Gardens that already have a location update to it once, the next time the app opens online.
Credits lists the ERA5 records.
Leftover Japanese wording is gone: adding a crop of your own no longer asks for a Japanese name, and the place search, seed company and feeding examples are general.
The forecast strip spans the full width again with its 6 days, and the Open-Meteo credit sits above it in small italics.

The forecast uses far fewer requests: one small request (7 hourly values over 7 days — yesterday and the next 6 — with each day’s high, low, rain and wind worked out from the hours), fetched at most every 3 hours and only while the app is on screen. The forecast strip shows today and the next 5 days.

Credits (Tools, at the bottom): the weather and climate data (Open-Meteo, from Copernicus ERA5), place search (GeoNames) and fonts the app uses, with their licences. The forecast also credits Open-Meteo.

Plants in bed and pot drawings are drawn as their crop — a cabbage, a lettuce, a tomato — once each is a plant of its own: planted out, thinned, or (a sowing that isn’t thinned) come up. Before that, and where they’re too small to see or too many to draw, they stay as dots.

Going back returns you to where you were on the page — open a bag from halfway down the garden, go back, and you’re halfway down again (the ← button, the phone’s back, or the browser’s). Pages you open anew still start at the top.
Deleting a planting that came from your seedlings puts them back in their tray or pots — so a plant-out that went wrong can be undone and done again.

Guided setup: for a new garden, a card at the top of each page walks you through your first bed or pot and your first crop — raising seedlings in a tray first, or planting straight in — moving on by itself as you do each step, then shows what the app does for you. Start it from the first-run steps, or any time from Tools → Guided setup.

Planting out seedlings: the plants that go in are the ones the drawing holds, and only their cells or pots leave the tray. A 4-plant diamond in a grow bag takes 4 plants (2 cells at 2 a cell); the rest stay in the tray to replant elsewhere. If the layout has room for more than you have, it offers to place just yours, so the drawing and the number always match.
Drop-down lists stay open while you type in their search box on a phone (the keyboard opening used to close them).

New Zealand spinach grows from about 5 °C (it had the growth temperatures of water spinach, a tropical crop), and the feeding card no longer calls a cool late-spring spell “the slow winter stretch” — that’s only for real winter cold.

34 more crops, chosen for gardens worldwide (130 in all): butternut, acorn, gem, yellow and pattypan squash; pickling cucumbers; jalapeño, cayenne and habanero; tomatillo and ground cherry; parsnip, baby carrots, celeriac and swede; shallots; collards and savoy cabbage; endive, radicchio, corn salad, perpetual spinach, amaranth greens and New Zealand spinach; climbing, runner, lima, dry and cowpea beans; popcorn; Thai basil, flat-leaf parsley, chervil and Florence fennel.

Each grows as its own crop: habanero needs more heat than other chillies, runner beans stop setting in hot summers, swedes and corn salad need cool weather to mature, parsnips and celeriac are spring-sown long-season roots, and so on — every one checked in Japan, Sydney, Melbourne, London, Singapore, Denver, Johannesburg, Cape Town, Durban and 90 made-up climates.
The last “Fushokufu” in the crop ideas is now “fleece”.

Frost-tender crops planted as spring warms (potatoes) are only offered where they’d come up after the usual last frost — no more June–July potatoes on the Johannesburg highveld. Where winters are mild the potato season runs longer, up to where the tubers would fill in the heat (Johannesburg: August–October).
Crops planted to go through winter (garlic, onions, peas, broad beans) are never offered at the top of summer where summers are cool: London’s garlic is now September–October instead of August.

Behind the scenes, every crop is now checked in 90 made-up climates — both hemispheres, winters from −10 °C to tropical, summers from cool to hot, with frost where it would come — against rules that hold anywhere: harvest within the year, frost-tender crops between the frosts, nothing maturing in heat or days long enough to bolt it. Plus Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban against local growing guides.

English only: Japanese crop names, the crop-name language switch, Japanese glosses in jobs and advice (“Earth up (土寄せ)” is now “Earth up”), the Japanese solar terms and the built-in variety lists (Japanese varieties) are gone. Varieties you’ve entered are still suggested.

Crop names in plain English where there’s a common one: Chinese cabbage (napa), Cherry tomato, Welsh onion (long white), Shishito pepper, Shungiku (edible chrysanthemum), Yard-long bean, Winter melon, Chinese yam, Turnip greens (nozawana) and others. Names that are the usual ones in English stay: daikon, komatsuna, mizuna, edamame, shiso…
Fushokufu is now “fleece” (row cover).

“The usual home-garden crops” is a worldwide list: tomatoes, lettuce, carrots, beetroot, radish, onions, garlic, potatoes, beans, peas, zucchini, cucumber, capsicum, chilli, pumpkin, sweetcorn, spinach, chard, kale, cabbage, broccoli, basil and parsley.
Jobs the app had already written in your garden lose their Japanese glosses too; your own notes are untouched.

No built-in products any more: there are far too many in the world. New gardens start with none — add the fertilisers, composts, potting mixes and sprays you use. Yours, including any you had from the old built-in list, are kept as your own entries.

Sprays work from what you enter from the label: the crops it’s for, and for each the days to wait before picking and the most sprays allowed a season. The app looks nothing up — it says so wherever sprays appear. Logging a spray checks the crops you sprayed against what you entered and counts the sprays left; the waiting period still holds picking.

Sprays you had that came with Japan’s register data keep those crops, waits and limits as your own; your stochu recipe is in that product’s notes. The register lookup, legal notices, mixing helper and Japanese product details are gone.
A product your records mention is kept out of sight when you remove it, so what you recorded still counts.

Test site only — Time travel (Tools → Test site): move the test garden to another date (±1, 7 or 30 days, or any date) to see how plantings, jobs, feeding and harvests play out. The whole app takes that as today, and the badge at the top shows the date.

While travelling, the weather is what it actually did on those days: that year’s records, or — for days still to come — the same days in the latest year that has them. “Back to today” returns and drops the borrowed weather. The real site never moves.
Labels on the bed and pot drawings (crop names, “+ empty”) have a thin even outline again, instead of dark overlapping bubbles round each letter when a bed or small pot is drawn large.

Tools → Delete all my data: removes your garden from this phone — beds and pots, plantings, records, photos, products, settings and the daily recovery copies — and starts the app again as new. It first reminds you to back up (showing when you last did, with a button to export one now), then only deletes once you type DELETE. Backup files and Google Drive backups are kept; on the test site only the test garden is deleted.
Buttons that redraw the page you’re on (like the hemisphere tabs in Tools → Weather & climate) no longer fold up every section or jump the page: open sections stay open and you stay where you were.
Tapping a hemisphere before picking a climate type no longer switches the climate by itself — it applies when you pick the type.

No location, or offline? Pick your climate type instead (Tools → Weather & climate, or the first-run “Where” step): eleven Köppen–Geiger types from tropical to continental — humid subtropical in two, since Tokyo and Sydney share a type but not a winter — for either hemisphere. Each gives a typical year (with frost dates where frost is usual) for sowing months, growth and seasons.
Setting your location later replaces it with your own garden’s 10-year records; until they’re in, the picked type stands (and the home screen says so).

Day length now counts, worked out from your latitude. Daikon, hakusai, bok choy, komatsuna and mizuna aren’t offered for sowings that would mature in days of 15½ hours or more — they bolt instead (far from the equator only: London’s midsummer is 16.6 h, so there they’re sown from midsummer, as the RHS advises; Japan’s longest days are shorter).

When planting onions, the form says which type bulbs where you are: short-day near the tropics, short or intermediate at Japan’s and Sydney’s latitudes, long-day for spring planting further from the equator.
The “lengthening days make it flower” warning follows the actual day length (past 12 hours and getting longer), so it comes at the right time of year south of the equator too.

Real frost dates for your location: the climate now also reads the daily lows of the last 10 years and works out when frosts usually start and end (Tools → Weather & climate shows them). Where frost only comes some winters, it says so and doesn’t set the seasons by it.

Frost-tender crops are offered for planting only after the usual last frost, and must finish — or, for crops picked over weeks, stop picking — by the usual first one. Autumn potatoes end at the first frost there, instead of when the average temperature falls to about 8.5 °C (which comes too late where nights get much colder than days, like Denver).
Your climate is fetched again once to add the frost dates.

Sowing months now work for gardens anywhere, not just Japan. Warm-season crops go by their own temperatures: they must keep growing (no spell below about 14 °C for tomatoes, corn and beans, 16 °C for eggplant, okra and melons) and, sown as it cools, crop in weather warm enough to set and ripen. Before, one 12 °C limit let tomatoes, corn and beans through all year where winters are mild — Sydney.

Crops planted to go through winter (garlic, onions, peas, broad beans) and crops planted as spring warms (potatoes) move with how mild the winter is: Sydney’s garlic goes in March–May (not January), onions May–June, potatoes in August as well as late summer; Okinawa’s onions in December. Garlic can now be autumn-planted where winters are hard (Hokkaido, Denver: October).
In the tropics, warm-season crops can go in any month (no autumn to beat). Japan’s own sowing chart is only leaned on where the weather is like central Japan’s.
No crop is counted as ready in much under two-thirds of its packet days, however warm it is.
South of the equator, the rotation plan names seasons like “2026–27” (July to June, by when a crop was planted), and the Problems helper shifts Japan’s pest seasons by six months.
Behind the scenes, every crop is now checked in Sydney, Melbourne, London, Singapore and Denver as well as Japan, including against months local growing guides give.

Setting your garden’s location now fetches the usual weather there straight away. Before, it waited until the app was next opened, and until then sowing months, growth, harvest and feeding times quietly used western Tokyo’s climate (so a Sydney garden got a “slow winter stretch” in January).

While it isn’t in yet (offline, or the fetch failed), the home screen and sowing calendar say so, with ↻ Get it now. A climate fetched for a different place no longer counts after you move the location.
The Japanese solar terms (立冬 “Start of winter” …) are only shown for gardens in Japan.

Covers now count in growth times. While fushokufu is on, the section under it grows as if about 2.5 °C warmer in cool weather — an insect net a little (about 0.5 °C), shade cloth not at all — less as it warms up, and none from about 22 °C. Sprouting, thinning, harvest and feeding dates for that section come sooner; taking the cover off (its “off” date) ends it.
Crop ideas that say “or sow now under a tunnel or Fushokufu” now give the finish date with the cover counted.

Opening the app at its folder address (…/garden-planner/ or …/garden-planner/test/) moves to its own page, so Chrome sees it as the app it belongs to — for installing the test site next to the real one.

38 more crops, each grown like a close relative but with its own timings, spacing and season: tatsoi, mibuna, karashina, takana, nozawana, kosaitai, kohlrabi, Brussels sprouts, red cabbage, romanesco, stem broccoli, kailan, mini hakusai, leaf / sunny / romaine / butterhead lettuce, okahijiki, Malabar spinach, dill, egoma, bunching onion, wakegi, eshalot, leek, green peas, yard-long bean, black soybean, soybean, azuki, makuwa melon, winter melon, luffa, spaghetti squash, paprika, medium tomato, yacon and Chinese yam — 96 crops in all.
Spray registrations only show for a crop where they're certain to apply to it.

20 more crops, each fully described: okra, bitter melon (goya), pumpkin (kabocha), watermelon, melon, peanut, burdock (gobo), ginger, shiso, basil, kale, beetroot, rocket, coriander, molokhia, water spinach, mitsuba, parsley, rakkyo and Swiss chard — with their sowing months for your climate, timings, feeding, care jobs and pests.
A new Herbs group when choosing your crops.
Behind the scenes: everything the app knows about each crop is now kept together in one place, and checked automatically, ready for many more crops. Nothing should look different.

A new garden starts with a few welcome steps: what the app does (and that your garden stays on your phone), restoring a backup, where your garden is, which crops you grow, your first bed or pot, and how to keep a backup. All can be skipped and changed later.

My crops (Tools): choose the crops you grow. They come first in every crop list (the rest are under “Other crops”), and the sowing calendar and crop ideas are about them. Until you choose, everything is shown as before.
Drop-down lists show headings where a list is grouped.

Timings follow your climate properly: packet days are for central Japan, so cooler places now take longer and warmer ones less (they came out the same everywhere before). Crops usually grown through winter, sown in spring where winters are hard (onions, peas in Hokkaido), take months, not most of a year.
Taro planted in April is ready in about 6 months (it showed almost a year): sprouting time now follows the soil warming over the following weeks, not just the planting day.
Sowing months are only offered where the crop can finish in time: no taro in Hokkaido, no mid-August corn in Tokyo.
Behind the scenes: every crop is now checked automatically, sown in every month it's offered, in four climates (Tokyo, Sapporo, Kagoshima, Naha), for timings that don't make sense.

A crop of your own now says which crop it's most like (tatsoi → komatsuna, okahijiki → spinach…). Everything you don't give — spacing, sowing months, growth, time to planting out, feeding, care jobs, pests, even its icon — comes from that crop, and what you give from the packet wins.
Crops of your own you added before show "not linked" in Products & seeds → Seeds & plants: edit one to choose what it's like.
Spray registrations don't carry over from the crop it's like: a spray registered for komatsuna isn't registered for tatsoi.
The test site can be installed as an app of its own, next to the real one (Chrome said it was already installed). The real app stays the same app on your phone.

Every crop has its own response to temperature — the cold below which it stops growing and the warmth at which it grows at full speed — instead of three groups. Eggplant, peppers and cucumbers now need more warmth than tomatoes and beans; celery and potatoes stop sooner in the cold than lettuce.

Crops of your own take their growing temperatures from the packet (生育適温, e.g. 15–25 °C) — when you add one, or with "edit this crop" in Products & seeds → Seeds & plants. Without them, their dates count plain days, and the crop says so.

Every crop has its own time to planting out and the sign it's ready — spinach about 3 weeks in mild weather, planted out young at 2–3 true leaves — instead of a stand-in figure for crops that didn't have one. Root crops, potatoes, taro, sweet potatoes and garlic say they aren't raised in trays.
The signs are in English ("at 4–5 true leaves").
For a crop of your own, starting seedlings asks for its days to planting out (from the packet); until then there's no plant-out date rather than a guess.
Crop ideas no longer suggest planting out heat-bolting crops (spinach, lettuce…) as the weather warms into summer.
Moving seedlings (indoors, under cover, outside): the card says where they are and since when — "outside since 23 Nov" — and editing asks the day you moved them.
The plant-out date counts the days they spent indoors as indoor days, instead of working it out as if they'd been in their new spot all along.

Seedlings that fill gaps now show in the planting's drawing, at their own (younger) size — move them to where they really are, and take out any that didn't make it, with Arrange plants by hand. A gap filled before this shows a "show it in the drawing" button.

Seedlings two (or more) to a pot or cell: say how many plants go in each new pot when you replant, and how many each holds when you start seedlings. Planting out a pot then plants all of its seedlings.

Replanting seedlings into a bed or bag where the same crop is already growing offers "fill gaps": they join that planting (replacing ones that didn't come up), instead of making a second planting of it. The planting shows when its gaps were filled.
Already planted some out as a separate planting next to the same crop? Its page offers to add them to the first one.
Placing seedlings by hand starts with the number you're planting out.
Seedlings you raised from seed are drawn by their real age (from sowing in the tray), so they no longer look bigger than older plants sown in the ground.

Seedlings: one Replant button instead of "Plant out" and "Pot on". Choose how many and when, then where: a bed, bag or pot in the garden, or another tray or pots to grow on. The rest stay where they are.

Your own tray and pot sizes, as many as you use: a 49-cell and a 9-cell tray side by side, 9 cm and 12 cm pots… Add or change them on the Seedlings page, or add a new size right where you choose the tray.
Planting seedlings out into a bed, bag or pot where something is already growing works: they go where you say. (Other new plantings ask once instead of refusing.)
A few seedlings into a bag or pot are drawn as that many plants.
Seedlings in trays and pots get the same looks as seeds in a bed: how many cells are up (or count them), again every few days until they're up — and planting out waits until they are.
Pot on: move some seedlings from a tray into 9 cm pots. They become their own group on the Seedlings page, to plant out later; the rest stay in the tray.
Plant out a few at a time into different beds, bags or pots — each lot becomes its own planting, and what's left stays in the tray. Discarding some keeps a note of why.
Crops sown in a continuous line are drawn as their sowing lines, widening as they grow, without a dot for every seed. Arranging plants by hand comes once they're thinned.

Crops sown in a continuous line (spinach, carrots, komatsuna…): when you look at how many have come up, count the seedlings along 10 cm of row instead of being told there are hundreds of "spots" — the app works out the share from how thickly it was sown.
A planting sown in a continuous line shows about how many plants it will be once thinned.

Checking that seeds have come up is now a few looks, not one answer: each time, say roughly how many are up (None yet, A few, A quarter… or a percentage, or count them), and when you looked. You can add a look from the planting's page too.

Nothing up yet? The app asks again in 3 days, and doesn't plan thinning until they're up — harvest is counted from when they do come up. Some crops (spinach especially) can take weeks in cold soil; re-sowing is only suggested once it's taking far longer than usual.

Some up? It asks again every few days until most are up or the number stops changing, then offers re-sowing the gaps. When they came up is worked out from your looks, and thinning and harvest follow it.
Your earlier answers are kept: a "Nothing came up" from the last few weeks becomes your first look, with the next one due now.

After answering a pop-up (like "Save the plan anyway?" or "Delete this planting?"), the app no longer sometimes jumps back to the page you were on — e.g. back to the planting form after the planting had already been saved, where saving again would make a second one.
Arranging plants by hand works again in beds with a net or other cover over them: taps go through the cover to the plants, and a tap close to a plant counts.

Products & seeds (Tools, the 📦 tile) has a tab for each kind of product, and a Seeds & plants tab for your varieties — each with its seed packet photos, used again whenever you plant that variety. Adding a variety of a crop the app doesn't know adds the crop too.
Watering jobs for everything you grow: each bed in the ground (watered much less often than pots — the soil holds far more), indoor pots and seedlings, as well as pots & bags.
Watering follows the latest forecast: it's fetched again whenever you open the app or come back to it, so a forecast that changes (say, rain that's no longer coming) changes the jobs too.

Care jobs follow growth, not the calendar: a cold spell pushes them back, and supports (nets, trellises, stakes) for crops that go through winter — like autumn-sown peas — go up in spring when they start climbing.
Seedlings: "Buy them" or "Sow from seed"; a planting that uses seedlings you started shows them instead.
Thinning advice is in English, and pre-filled for you to change.
The spray days page warns about bee-harmful ingredients in any product (neonicotinoids, pyrethroids, organophosphates and more), and lists which of your sprays have them.
Drop-down lists stay with their field when a pop-up scrolls.
Drop-down lists open right under the field again (crops, products and so on), instead of the phone's own picker or the bar above the keyboard.
Deleting something asks "are you sure?" again.
Both had stopped working in 1.26.0.

If your garden ever can't be loaded, a Recovery screen helps instead: keep a copy of what's stored, go back to one of this phone's daily copies, restore a backup file, or start again — nothing is saved over your garden while it can't be loaded.
Restoring a backup (file, daily copy or Google Drive) can be undone from Tools → Backup, and your photos are no longer cleared before a restore.
Backups made by older versions of the app are tested with every change, so they keep restoring correctly.
The app tells you when a newer version is out, with what's new, and shows what changed after it updates.
There's now a separate test site for trying out changes first, with its own data.
Very large beds no longer freeze the app; bed and pot sizes are checked as you type.
The garden map can zoom in when a big bed makes everything else tiny.
The ruler along beds no longer shows 0, never crowds, and round pots have none.
Behind the scenes: the app's code was reorganised so it's easier to keep working well. Nothing should look different.
